Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern have urged the Surface Transportation Board to continue reviewing their proposed merger, pushing back against Canadian Pacific Kansas City’s request to terminate the proceeding as four rail labor organizations endorsed the transaction.
The proposed combination would create what the companies describe as the nation’s first single-line, seamless coast-to-coast railroad. Its review has drawn competing arguments over potential freight growth, employment protections, customer choice and whether stakeholders can voice objections without fear of retaliation.
A flurry of filings marked the Nov. 19 deadline for public comments.
In their response to CPKC (NYSE: CP ), Union Pacific (NYSE: UNP ) and Norfolk Southern (NYSE: NSC ) said they support a full, transparent and rigorous regulatory review and encourage stakeholders to make their views known to the STB.
Reiterating comments he made earlier to FreightWaves, UP issued its first public statement regarding remarks by Chief Executive Jim Vena at a shippers conference threatening rate hikes for shippers who didn’t support the merger.
“I do use humor in my presentations to keep the audience engaged, including in my presentation at the conference of the Southwest Association of Rail Shippers this past March,” Vena said. “I know what I said and regret the inference.”
Vena said the speech lasted more than 50 minutes and that he attempted humor near its conclusion.
“I apologize to anyone who misunderstood my statement,” he said.
Four labor organizations support merger
Separately, the SMART Transportation Division, the National Conference of Firemen and Oilers, the International Brotherhood of Boilermakers and SMART’s Mechanical Division submitted joint comments urging the STB to approve the merger.
Each organization has secured a “Jobs for Life” agreement with Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern. The agreements provide career-long employment commitments for covered workers, subject to their respective terms, and depend on approval and completion of the transaction.
“For generations, railroaders have been asked to carry the uncertainty while somebody else makes the decisions,” SMART-TD President Jeremy Ferguson said. “We went to the bargaining table and secured binding commitments to our members’ futures.”
For covered SMART-TD members, the protections include safeguards against involuntary furlough in their crafts, under their collective bargaining agreements and within their current seniority districts. The other organizations negotiated protections tailored to the workers they represent.
The coalition urged regulators to approve the transaction with the employment commitments honored in full, effective safety and service oversight, and continued labor involvement during implementation.
The labor organizations argue that a more connected network, fewer interchange delays and more dependable service could help railroads compete for freight now moving by truck.
Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern estimate that the combined network could shift approximately 2.1 million truckloads from highways to rail annually.
The unions contend that winning that freight would generate more railroad work while potentially reducing highway congestion and heavy-truck traffic.
“Every load we win back to rail is an opportunity for railroaders to show what we do best,” said Michael Pistone, president of the National Conference of Firemen and Oilers. “America needs a supply chain that can carry more freight safely and reliably.”
Chemical industry raises retaliation concerns
The American Chemistry Council raised a different concern, saying the application’s size and the review standards are not the only factors distinguishing the proceeding.
“This merger application differs from many that have come before it — not only because of its magnitude and the new standards of review, but also because it is being considered under a dark cloud amid concerns about potential retaliation against those who speak out,” the council said.
CN seeks competitive-access conditions
Canadian National (NYSE: CNI ) has filed proposed conditions with the STB aimed at preserving customer options and expanding its access in several Midwest markets. The proposals build on a framework negotiated with Union Pacific.
CN’s requested conditions focus on four areas:
Kansas City: Acquiring Union Pacific’s Kansas City–St. Louis line and securing access to Neff Yard.
St. Louis and East St. Louis: Improving connectivity and rail access, including shorter routes for certain shipments.
Des Moines and Avon, Iowa: Preserving access to at least two Class I railroads for affected customers.
Illinois: Protecting existing rail competition and customer choice.
In their July announcement, CN and Union Pacific said they had signed a binding memorandum of understanding covering competitive access, terminal railroad ownership and expanded Midwest operating rights. The agreement is contingent on STB approval and completion of the merger; CN also agreed not to oppose the transaction.
That framework includes CN acquiring Norfolk Southern’s interests in the Kansas City Terminal Railway and Terminal Railroad Association of St. Louis, along with new access rights in the Midwest and use of Union Pacific’s Neff Yard.
The STB is expected render a decision on the merger in 2027.
Why it matters: The proposed merger if approved is likely to reshape North American logistics, but questions remain as to whether a coast-to-coast network can deliver the service improvements and freight growth its proponents project.
